sites.s: Bronze Age towers and tombs · World Heritage
sites.se: Round stone buildings 20 m wide whose purpose is still unknown, and a hillside of beehive tombs
sites.sa: مبانٍ حجرية دائرية بعرض 20 م لا يُعرف غرضها، وسفح من قبور كخلايا النحل
sites.desc: A 3rd-millennium BC necropolis and settlement in Al Dhahirah: at Bat about 100 graves and circular buildings each about 20 m in diameter with no outside openings; at Al-Khutm, 2 km west, a rock tower of 20 m thought to be a fort; and at Al-Ayn, 22 km south-east, the best-preserved line of beehive tombs on a ridge. A Danish team under Karen Frifelt excavated in 1972 and found some 4,000 years of continuous occupation. Inscribed in 1988 under criteria (iii) and (iv), Oman's second World Heritage site.
sites.sig: The most complete Bronze Age settlement and cemetery landscape of the 3rd millennium BC in the world, per UNESCO.
sites.ex: Danish expedition (K. Frifelt) 1972; University of Pennsylvania Bat Archaeological Project 2007–2012
disc: Circular towers 20 m across without doors
refs: Thornton, C. P., Cable, C. M. & Possehl, G. L. (2016). The Bronze Age Towers at Bat, Sultanate of Oman. University of Pennsylvania Press.

sites.s: Mud-brick fortress of the Banu Nabhan · World Heritage
sites.se: A mud-brick fortress and a 13 km wall around an oasis famous for its potters
sites.sa: قلعة من الطوب الطيني وسور بطول 13 كم حول واحة اشتهرت بخزّافيها
sites.desc: A fortress of mud brick and straw at the foot of the Jebel Akhdar, believed to have been built between the 12th and 15th centuries by the Banu Nabhan, with the Al-Qasabah as its oldest part, the Bait al-Hadith of the Ya'ariba dynasty (1624–1743) and the 18th-century Bait al-Jabal. A wall of about 13 km, partly standing, encloses the oasis. Inscribed in 1987 as Oman's first World Heritage site, placed on the List in Danger from 1988 to 2004 because of decay of the unfired brick, and reopened in 2012 after a long restoration.
sites.sig: The largest surviving earthen fortress of the Gulf and a lesson in how to conserve mud architecture.
sites.ex: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism; ArCHIAM Centre management plan 2013
disc: Three building phases from the 12th to the 18th century
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Bahla Fort (ref. 433), inscribed 1987; State of Conservation report 2018.

sites.s: Frankincense port · World Heritage
sites.se: A walled port founded by the kings of Hadramawt to ship frankincense to Rome and India
sites.sa: ميناء مسوّر أسسه ملوك حضرموت لشحن اللبان إلى روما والهند
sites.desc: A fortified port on a lagoon east of Salalah, founded at the end of the 1st century BC by the kingdom of Hadramawt to control the Dhofar incense trade, and identified with the Moscha of classical texts. Inscriptions in the gate name the city Sumhuram; warehouses, a temple and houses lie within the walls. One of four components of the Land of Frankincense property (849.88 ha) inscribed in 2000 under criteria (iii) and (iv) and renamed in 2005.
sites.sig: The best-preserved pre-Islamic port of the incense route, where South Arabian script meets Roman and Indian trade.
sites.ex: American Foundation for the Study of Man 1952–53; Italian Mission to Oman (University of Pisa) 1997 onwards
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Land of Frankincense (ref. 1010), inscribed 2000.
Avanzini, A. (ed.) (2008). A Port in Arabia between Rome and the Indian Ocean (3rd C. BC – 5th C. AD): Khor Rori Report 2. L'Erma di Bretschneider.

sites.s: Medieval port of Dhofar · World Heritage
sites.el: Port with citadel and grand mosque
sites.se: A walled medieval port that sold frankincense and horses to China and India
sites.sa: ميناء مسوّر من العصور الوسطى باع اللبان والخيول للصين والهند
sites.desc: The ruins of the medieval city of Zafar on the Salalah shore: a walled port with a citadel and a grand mosque, visited by Ibn Battuta and recorded by Marco Polo's generation, which exported frankincense and Arabian horses across the Indian Ocean until its decline in the 16th century. It is a component of the Land of Frankincense World Heritage property and houses the Museum of the Frankincense Land.
sites.sig: The medieval successor of Sumhuram and the last great port of the incense trade.
sites.ex: Office of the Adviser to His Majesty for Cultural Affairs; German (DAI) and American missions
disc: Horse-export port of the Middle Ages
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Land of Frankincense (ref. 1010).

sites.s: Caravan oasis of the incense road
sites.el: Spring and collapsed fort at the desert edge
sites.te: The city lost in the sands
sites.se: A caravan fort over a spring, identified in the 1990s with the legendary Ubar
sites.sa: حصن قوافل فوق عين، رُبط في التسعينيات بمدينة أوبار الأسطورية
sites.desc: A spring and fortified caravan station on the edge of the Rub' al Khali north of Thumrait, part of the incense trade network by 300 BC. Identified in the early 1990s by Sir Ranulph Fiennes and a team of archaeologists as the legendary Ubar, an identification still debated; part of the fort collapsed into the sinkhole of its own spring. A component of the Land of Frankincense World Heritage property.
sites.sig: The desert end of the incense road, where caravans watered before crossing to the Gulf.
sites.ex: Trans-Arabia Expedition (N. Clapp, R. Fiennes, J. Zarins) 1990–1995
disc: Fort collapsed into its spring sinkhole

sites.n: Falaj Daris and the Aflaj of Oman
sites.s: Living irrigation channels · World Heritage
sites.el: Five inscribed aflaj; c. 3,000 still flowing
sites.se: Underground channels up to 12 km long bring mountain water to oases, still divided by the stars
sites.sa: قنوات تحت الأرض بطول 12 كم تجلب ماء الجبل إلى الواحات، وما زالت تُقسَّم بالنجوم
sites.desc: Falaj Daris at Nizwa is the largest of five aflaj inscribed in 2006 (with Al-Khatmeen, Al-Malki, Al-Mayassar and Al-Jeela) under criterion (v). About 3,000 aflaj still function in Oman; the systems date from around AD 500 within a 5,000-year irrigation tradition. Daudi aflaj (23.5%) run underground up to 12 km and 50 m deep; ghaili aflaj (48.5%) are seasonal open channels; aini aflaj (28%) carry spring water, sometimes hot. Water is shared by timed turns under a management system that has survived for centuries.
sites.sig: The most extensive living example of ancient water engineering in Arabia.
sites.ex: Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources (Aflaj inventory)
disc: Daudi channels up to 12 km long
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman (ref. 1207), inscribed 2006.
Al-Ghafri, A. S. (2018). Overview about the aflaj of Oman. Proceedings of the International Symposium of Khettaras and Qanats.

sites.s: Hormuz-era port · World Heritage
sites.se: A port that Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta praised, ruled by a woman after 1311
sites.sa: ميناء أثنى عليه ماركو بولو وابن بطوطة، حكمته امرأة بعد عام 1311
sites.desc: The ruins of a walled port of more than 24 ha north of Sur, the second city of the Kingdom of Hormuz. Marco Polo called it Calatu in the 13th century and Ibn Battuta in the 14th praised its bazaars and a mosque built by Bibi Maryam, who ruled Qalhat and Hormuz after her husband Ayaz died in 1311–12; her mausoleum, now without its dome, is the main standing monument. The city declined as trade moved to Muscat, was taken by the Portuguese by 1507, and earthquakes on the Qalhat Fault are a plausible cause of its ruin. Inscribed in 2018.
sites.sig: A rare intact medieval Indian Ocean port, abandoned early and never rebuilt.
sites.ex: French Archaeological Mission at Qalhat (A. Rougeulle), 2008 onwards
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Ancient City of Qalhat (ref. 1537), inscribed 2018.
Rougeulle, A. (ed.) (2017). Qalhāt, Oman: a medieval port city. Archaeopress.

sites.na: قرية رأس الجنز من العصر البرونزي
sites.s: Fishing village in contact with the Indus
sites.se: A village at the easternmost point of Arabia that traded with India 4,000 years ago
sites.sa: قرية في أقصى شرق الجزيرة العربية تاجرت مع الهند قبل 4,000 عام
sites.desc: Remains covering about 1 km² at the easternmost point of Arabia, 11 km south of Ras al Hadd, with 100 documented sites and some 350 graves on the mesa above Khawr Jarama. Occupation runs from the early Holocene to the Iron Age; steatite vessels date to about 2300 BC, an incense burner to 2200 BC and settlements to 2000 BC. A potsherd with a Harappan inscription found in 1982 shows contact with the Indus Valley, with bitumen, stamp seals, fish hooks, metal pins and an Indian ivory comb among the finds. On the UNESCO Tentative List with the turtle reserve (2013).
sites.sig: Evidence that Oman's fishermen were part of the Bronze Age world linking Mesopotamia, the Gulf and the Indus.
sites.ex: Joint Hadd Project (S. Cleuziou, M. Tosi), 1985–2000s
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Ras al Had Turtle Reserve and the Heritage Site of Ras al Jinz, Tentative List ref. 5840 (2013).
Cleuziou, S. & Tosi, M. (2007). In the Shadow of the Ancestors: the prehistoric foundations of the early Arabian civilization in Oman. Ministry of Heritage and Culture.

sites.s: The world’s largest slice of ocean crust on land
sites.dr: Crust formed 96 – 94 million years ago; thrust onto Arabia soon after
sites.el: 550 km long · 150 km wide · over 10,000 km²
sites.te: The sea floor that climbed onto the land
sites.ta: قاع البحر الذي صعد إلى اليابسة
sites.se: Oman’s dark mountains are a 550 km sheet of oceanic crust and mantle pushed over the continent
sites.sa: جبال عُمان الداكنة صفيحة من قشرة المحيط ووشاحه بطول 550 كم دُفعت فوق القارة
sites.desc: The Hajar Mountains are built largely of the Semail ophiolite, described as the world's largest and best-preserved thrust sheet of oceanic crust and upper mantle: more than 10,000 km², about 550 km long and 150 km wide. The crust formed 96–94 million years ago at a spreading centre above a north-east-dipping subduction zone and was emplaced onto the Arabian margin in the Late Cretaceous; its metamorphic sole formed at about 850 °C 95–93 million years ago, and eclogites at As Sifah record continental crust dragged 78–90 km down. The sequence, from arc lavas and pillow basalts through gabbros to more than 12 km of mantle harzburgite, can be walked across in a day in wadis such as Wadi Al Abyad.
sites.sig: The reference ophiolite of the planet, where geologists go to see the ocean floor and the mantle at the surface.
sites.ex: Oxford (M. Searle) and international teams; Oman Drilling Project 2017–2018
disc: Mantle rock exposed at the surface
Eclogites from 78–90 km depth at As Sifah
refs: Searle, M. & Cox, J. Tectonic setting, origin, and obduction of the Oman ophiolite. Geological Society of America Bulletin 111(1), 104–122 (1999).

sites.s: Oman’s highest peak and its Grand Canyon
sites.dr: Limestone laid down 270 – 90 million years ago
sites.te: Three thousand metres of sea floor
sites.ta: ثلاثة آلاف متر من قاع البحر
sites.se: A canyon a kilometre deep cuts through the whole Hajar Supergroup
sites.sa: أخدود بعمق كيلومتر يشق مجموعة الحجر الكبرى بأكملها
sites.desc: At 3,010 m Jebel Shams is the highest point of the Jebel Akhdar and of Oman, in a range about 700 km long. Wadi Nakhr, the 'Grand Canyon of Arabia', is 12 km long, over 1 km wide at the viewpoint and more than 1,000 m deep, cutting through about 3,000 m of the Hajar Supergroup, shallow-marine limestone deposited from the Late Permian to the Late Cretaceous: Jurassic Sahtan oolitic limestone, Lower Cretaceous Kahmah limestone and marl, and the mid-Cretaceous Natih limestone over Nahr Umr shale, the same reservoir rocks that hold Oman's oil.
sites.sig: The clearest exposure of the rocks beneath Arabia's oil fields, visible from a single viewpoint.
sites.ex: Petroleum Development Oman geological surveys; GeoExpro (Whaley 2018)
refs: Whaley, J. (2018). The Grand Canyon of the Middle East. GEO ExPro, 3 December 2018.

sites.s: One of the largest cave chambers on Earth
sites.dr: Chamber in Middle Eocene Dammam limestone
sites.te: The meeting place of the spirits
sites.se: A chamber big enough to hold ten jumbo jets, entered only by rope through holes in its roof
sites.sa: قاعة تتسع لعشر طائرات جامبو، لا تُدخل إلا بالحبل عبر فتحات في سقفها
sites.desc: A single chamber about 310 m long, 225 m wide and 120 m high, with a floor of 58,000 m² and a volume of about 4 million m³, beneath the Selma Plateau at 1,380 m, 100 km south-east of Muscat. Formed in fossiliferous marly limestone of the Middle Eocene Dammam Formation under a roof only 40 m thick, it is entered by free descent through three ceiling holes (Cheryl's Drop 158 m, Asterisk 140 m, First Drop 118 m). Discovered in June 1983 by Don Davison and Cheryl Jones and surveyed in 1985, when it ranked second in the world by volume; it has been closed by the government since 2008.
sites.sig: A world-ranking cave chamber, and the same Dammam Formation that forms the aquifer of Bahrain and Qatar.
refs: Public Authority for Water Resources, Oman (1985). Report PAWR 85-20.
Davison, W. D. (1990). Meeting place of the spirits. Aramco World, Sept–Oct 1990.

sites.s: A sand sea 180 km long
sites.dr: Dunes formed after the last ice age
sites.se: Living dunes 100 m high rest on an older desert turned to stone
sites.sa: كثبان حيّة بارتفاع 100 م تستقر فوق صحراء أقدم تحوّلت إلى حجر
sites.desc: A dune field of about 12,500 km², 180 km north–south and 80 km east–west, whose northern dunes rise to 100 m and rest on an older layer of cemented carbonate sand. The 1986 Royal Geographical Society expedition recorded 16,000 invertebrates, 200 other animal species and 150 native plants, including ghaf (Prosopis cineraria) woodland; Bedouin of the Al Wahiba and other tribes still gather at the Al-Huyawah oasis for the date harvest.
sites.sig: One of the best-studied sand seas in the world and the type example of a dune field in the monsoon belt.
sites.ex: Royal Geographical Society Oman Wahiba Sands Project, 1985–1987
disc: Cemented sand beneath the living dunes
refs: Dutton, R. W. (ed.) (1988). The Scientific Results of the Royal Geographical Society's Oman Wahiba Sands Project 1985–1987. Journal of Oman Studies Special Report 3.

sites.s: Green turtle rookery
sites.se: Most of Oman’s green turtles nest on one 45 km stretch of beach
sites.sa: تعشّش معظم سلاحف عُمان الخضراء على شريط شاطئ واحد بطول 45 كم
sites.desc: A 120 km² reserve declared on 23 April 1996 covering about 45 km of coast from Khawr Jarama to Ras Ruwais, with two lagoons, mangrove and coral at Khawr Jarama, about 130 bird species and the white stork on migration. About 20,000 green turtles nest on more than 275 beaches along Oman's coast and most nest within this reserve; 14 rangers and a visitor centre at Ras al-Jinz manage night viewing. On the UNESCO Tentative List since 2013 together with the Bronze Age site.
sites.sig: One of the largest green turtle nesting grounds in the Indian Ocean.
sites.ex: Environment Authority, Oman; Ras al-Jinz Scientific and Visitor Centre
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Ras al Had Turtle Reserve and the Heritage Site of Ras al Jinz, Tentative List ref. 5840 (2013).

sites.s: Globally important loggerhead rookery
sites.se: From 20,000–40,000 females a year to about 10,000, mostly lost to fishing nets
sites.sa: من 20 إلى 40 ألف أنثى في السنة إلى نحو 10 آلاف، فُقد معظمها في شباك الصيد
sites.desc: Masirah Island's 83 km of beaches hold one of the world's most important loggerhead turtle rookeries. Nesting females were estimated at 20,000–40,000 a year in 1977–1986 but at 10,223–11,500 in 2008–2016 (about 55,000 nests a year); track counts on the index beaches fell 79% between 1985–1996 and 2008–2016, within a single turtle generation of about 47 years, and density fell further by 2019. Bycatch is the most likely cause: community surveys in 2013 estimated 1,640–1,770 loggerheads a year caught in artisanal gillnets. Demersal trawling has been illegal in Oman since 2011.
sites.sig: A warning from the Indian Ocean's largest loggerhead population, measured over forty years.
sites.ex: Environment Authority, Oman with Five Oceans Environmental Services (Willson et al. 2020)
refs: Willson, A., Witherington, B., Baldwin, R., Tiwari, M., Al Sariri, T., Al Kiyumi, A. et al. (2020). Evaluating the long-term trend and management of a globally important loggerhead population nesting on Masirah Island, Sultanate of Oman. Frontiers in Marine Science 7, 666.

sites.s: Stronghold of the Arabian leopard
sites.se: A 4,500 km² escarpment above Dhofar where the Arabian leopard still breeds
sites.sa: جرف بمساحة 4,500 كم² فوق ظفار ما زال النمر العربي يتكاثر فيه
sites.desc: A reserve of about 4,500 km² on the Jabal Samhan escarpment of Dhofar, established by Royal Decree 48/97, where camera-trap surveys confirmed a persisting population of the critically endangered Arabian leopard and a mother with cub was recorded in 2022. It also holds Arabian wolf, striped hyena, Arabian gazelle, Nubian ibex, rock hyrax, honey badger and red fox, with frankincense, wild fig, wild olive and acacia on its slopes and the monsoon fog of the khareef on its seaward face.
sites.sig: The most important site on Earth for the Arabian leopard, with fewer than 200 left in the wild.
sites.ex: Office for Conservation of the Environment, Diwan of Royal Court (J. A. Spalton)
refs: Spalton, J. A., Al Hikmani, H. M., Willis, D. & Said, A. S. B. (2006). Critically endangered Arabian leopards Panthera pardus nimr persist in the Jabal Samhan Nature Reserve, Oman. Oryx 40(3), 287–294.
Oman Observer (17 August 2026). Jabal Samhan Nature Reserve protects rich biodiversity in Dhofar.

sites.s: Coral islands off Muscat
sites.te: Nine islands of birds and turtles
sites.se: Hawksbills, tropicbirds and corals on an archipelago reached only by boat
sites.sa: سلاحف منقار الصقر وطيور الاستوائي ومرجان على أرخبيل لا يُبلغ إلا بالقارب
sites.desc: Nine islands 16–18 km off the Batinah coast, declared a nature reserve on 3 April 1996 and submitted to the UNESCO Tentative List in 2013 under natural criterion (x). Some 250–300 hawksbill turtles nest each year and green turtles feed in the shallows; thousands of seabirds nest in summer, including red-billed tropicbird, osprey, roseate, white-cheeked, bridled and sooty terns and common noddy, over a multitude of coral species; humpback whales and dolphins pass offshore. Four rangers guard the islands and landing is restricted in the nesting season.
sites.sig: Oman's main hawksbill rookery and the richest coral site near the capital.
sites.ex: Environment Authority, Oman; Environment Society of Oman
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Al Dimaniyat Islands Nature Reserve, Tentative List ref. 5839 (2013).

sites.n: Al Wusta Wildlife Reserve (former Arabian Oryx Sanctuary)
sites.s: Where the oryx returned, and the listing was lost
sites.se: The first site ever removed from the World Heritage List, after the herd fell from 450 to 65
sites.sa: أول موقع يُحذف من قائمة التراث العالمي، بعد أن تراجع القطيع من 450 إلى 65
sites.desc: The gravel plain of Jiddat al-Harasis where Arabian oryx bred in captivity were returned to the wild from 1982, inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1994. Poaching and habitat degradation cut the free herd from about 450 in 1996 to 65 by 2007, with about four breeding pairs, and after Oman reduced the protected area by 90% to allow hydrocarbon prospecting the World Heritage Committee removed the site on 28 June 2007, the first deletion in the List's history. Oryx are now kept in fenced enclosures in what is today the Al Wusta Wildlife Reserve.
sites.sig: A global landmark in conservation history, both for the oryx's return and for its loss.
sites.ex: Office for Conservation of the Environment, Diwan of Royal Court
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2007). Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary: first site ever to be deleted from UNESCO's World Heritage List. News, 28 June 2007.
Spalton, J. A., Lawrence, M. W. & Brend, S. A. (1999). Arabian oryx reintroduction in Oman: successes and setbacks. Oryx 33(2).

sites.s: Frankincense trees · World Heritage
sites.el: Boswellia sacra woodland north of Salalah
sites.te: The trees that perfumed the ancient world
sites.se: Boswellia sacra still bleeds resin in a protected valley 45 minutes from Salalah
sites.sa: ما زالت شجرة اللبان تنزف صمغها في وادٍ محميّ على بعد 45 دقيقة من صلالة
sites.desc: A natural woodland of Boswellia sacra, the frankincense tree, in a dry valley about 45 minutes' drive north of Salalah, where resin is still tapped by cutting the bark as it was for the incense trade of Sumhuram and Zafar. The park is one of the four components of the Land of Frankincense World Heritage property inscribed in 2000.
sites.sig: The living source of the trade that built the ports of Dhofar.
sites.ex: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism; Office of the Adviser for Cultural Affairs
disc: Resin tapped by cutting the bark
Component of a World Heritage property
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Land of Frankincense (ref. 1010), inscribed 2000.

sites.s: The monsoon that greens Dhofar
sites.se: Fog from the Indian Ocean turns the mountains green and fills the waterfalls of Wadi Darbat
sites.sa: ضباب من المحيط الهندي يخضّر الجبال ويملأ شلالات وادي دربات
sites.desc: From late June to September the south-west monsoon wraps the Dhofar mountains in fog and drizzle, with the landscape greenest from mid-July to the end of August; temperatures drop while the rest of Arabia is at about 43 °C. Wadi Darbat, about 50 minutes from Salalah, fills with waterfalls, lakes and grazing camels, and the escarpment's woodland of figs, olives and frankincense depends on this fog. The season draws thousands of visitors to Salalah each year.
sites.sig: The only monsoon forest ecosystem of the Arabian Peninsula.
disc: Peak greenery mid-July to late August
refs: Hasan, D. (2023). Everything you need to know about travelling to Salalah during khareef season. The National, 20 July 2023.

sites.s: Bronze Age tower and Iron Age town near Bisya · Italian Mission to Oman
sites.p: Early Bronze Age to Iron Age (reused to the Islamic period)
sites.te: The hill where legends and layers meet
sites.ta: التلّ الذي تلتقي فيه الأساطير بالطبقات
sites.se: A fortified hill and a lower town near Bisya, dug since 2004 by an Italian mission, with a Bronze Age tower and an Iron Age settlement far larger than once thought
sites.sa: تلّ محصّن ومدينة سفلية قرب بسيا، تنقّب فيهما بعثة إيطالية منذ 2004، مع برج من العصر البرونزي ومستوطنة من العصر الحديدي أكبر بكثير مما كان يُظن
sites.desc: An ancient oasis on the Salut plain near Bisya in central Oman, first surveyed in the 1970s by Harvard University, the British Archaeological Expedition and the University of Birmingham, and excavated from 2004 by the Italian Mission to Oman (IMTO) led by Alessandra Avanzini. The mission rebuilt a collapsed Bronze Age tower, plastered the mud-brick walls for preservation and, after a decade of work, had restored the site's monumentality by 2015. Excavation of the lower settlement (Qaryat Salut) showed its inhabited area was much larger than previously thought, and very high radiocarbon dates from the upper fortified area (Husn Salut) point to a large central-Omani settlement by the end of the 2nd millennium BC with classic Iron Age material culture. Finds include pottery, soft-stone vessels, seals, bronze objects and terracotta figurines, presented in a Virtual Museum of Salut built by the mission.
sites.sig: Salut is the key excavated sequence for the Iron Age of central Oman, a region long overshadowed by sites in the UAE.
sites.ex: Italian Mission to Oman (University of Pisa, A. Avanzini) 2004–present; earlier surveys by Harvard, the British Archaeological Expedition and University of Birmingham
disc: Iron Age lower town far larger than previously thought
Bronze Age tower rebuilt after collapse

sites.s: Hafit-period towers with the oldest copper working in Oman · University of Tübingen
sites.el: Building V dated to about 3200 cal. BC
sites.ta: حيث صُهر النحاس في عُمان أول مرة
sites.se: One of the largest Early Bronze Age sites in Oman, 17 km north of Sinaw, whose stone tower holds the oldest substantial evidence of copper processing in the country
sites.sa: أحد أكبر مواقع العصر البرونزي المبكر في عُمان، على بعد 17 كم شمال سناو، يضم برجه الحجري أقدم دليل جوهري على معالجة النحاس في البلاد
sites.desc: Al-Khashbah, about 17 km north of Sinaw, is one of Oman's largest Early Bronze Age sites. The University of Tübingen excavated there for four seasons from 2015 to 2018 and uncovered Hafit-period architecture including a mud-brick complex (Building I, dated to about 2800 cal. BC) with bead and chipped-stone workshops, resembling the contemporary tower at Hili 8, and a stone tower (Building V) dated to about 3200 cal. BC. Building V holds the oldest substantial evidence of copper processing in Oman, which the excavators link to archaic Uruk texts that mention copper objects from the Arabian Gulf. The site has three Hafit-period stone towers and six Umm an-Nar-period towers, and the project, funded by the German Research Foundation, combined field, aerial and geophysical surveys with excavation.
sites.sig: It pushes the beginning of Omani copper metallurgy, the basis of the land of Magan, back to the end of the 4th millennium BC.
sites.ex: University of Tübingen (C. Schmidt, S. Döpper), 2015–2018
disc: Oldest substantial copper processing in Oman, c. 3200 BC
Mud-brick complex with bead workshops, c. 2800 BC

sites.s: Neolithic fishing village and shell midden in Muscat · Italian Archaeological Mission
sites.se: A shell-midden village on a promontory at Qurm, Muscat, where Neolithic fisher-gatherers lived year-round and buried their dead in a large cemetery
sites.sa: قرية من أكوام الأصداف على رأس بحري في القرم بمسقط، عاش فيها صيادون وجامعو أصداف من العصر الحجري الحديث طوال العام ودفنوا موتاهم في مقبرة كبيرة
sites.desc: RH-5 is a shell-midden settlement on a large promontory in the Qurm area of Muscat, excavated by the Italian Archaeological Mission in Oman with the support of the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism. It dates from the late 5th to the end of the 4th millennium BC and consists of superimposed food refuse from fishing, shell collecting, hunting and herding, together with dwellings, household installations, everyday objects and ornaments. Exploiting several ecological niches allowed year-round sedentary occupation. The excavations recovered 374 beads of stone and marine shell, and the site includes a large cemetery.
sites.sig: It is the reference site for the fisher-gatherer way of life that the excavators see as a key step in the neolithisation of Oman.

sites.s: Largest Early Iron Age hill fort in central Oman · German Mining Museum survey
sites.el: Fort surface of more than 20,000 m²
sites.te: A staircase up a mountain of stone
sites.se: A ruined stone fort about 175 m wide on a mountain top near the Lizq palm garden, reached by a stair up its northern face
sites.sa: حصن حجري متهدّم بعرض نحو 175 م على قمة جبل قرب بستان نخيل لزق، يُصعد إليه بدرج على واجهته الشمالية
sites.desc: The fort known as L1 stands on a mountain about 1,000 m south-east of the Lizq palm garden in Ash Sharqiyah North. The main fort on the western peak is about 175 m wide with a surface of more than 20,000 m², and stairs lead up the northern face of the mountain. Gerd Weisgerber of the German Mining Museum in Bochum discovered it in 1979, guided by Shaikh Hamdan al-Harthy of Samad, and in 1981 a single-season German team under Stephan Kroll mapped the site, carried out a small rescue excavation and restored the northern stairs. Kroll compared its pottery with Iron Age pottery from Iran; no falaj was found and the associated village has not been located.
sites.sig: It is described as the largest Early Iron Age fort in central Oman.
sites.ex: German Mining Museum, Bochum (G. Weisgerber 1979; S. Kroll 1981)

sites.s: Type-site of the Samad Late Iron Age · about 260 graves documented
sites.el: About 260 graves, Bronze Age to Late Iron Age
sites.se: An oasis cemetery in Sharqiyah where German excavations defined the non-writing Late Iron Age culture of central Oman
sites.sa: مقبرة واحة في الشرقية حدّدت فيها التنقيبات الألمانية ثقافة العصر الحديدي المتأخر غير الكاتبة في وسط عُمان
sites.desc: Samad al-Shan is an oasis about 2 km east of al-Maysar in Sharqiyah at 565 m altitude, discovered in part by British surveyors in 1976. From 1981 Gerd Weisgerber of the German Mining Museum in Bochum mapped it, and Burkhard Vogt, Weisgerber and Paul Yule excavated there; by the end of the project in 1995 about 210 of some 360 Late Iron Age graves had been investigated, and roughly 260 graves from the Bronze Age to the Late Iron Age were documented. The Samad assemblage, now known from 126 sites, is dated by absolute methods to about 300 BC – AD 300. Mature men were usually laid on the right side and women on the left; men's graves hold arrowheads, daggers and swords, women's never contain weapons, and imported glazed perfume bottles and lathe-turned soft-stone bowls appear with hand-made local pottery.
sites.sig: The site gives its name to the Late Iron Age of central Oman, a period otherwise without writing.

sites.s: 17th-century round tower of the Ya’ariba imams · Nizwa
sites.el: Tower about 36 m across and 30 m high
sites.te: A drum of stone over an underground stream
sites.ta: أسطوانة من حجر فوق جدول تحت الأرض
sites.se: A huge round tower built in the 1650s under Imam Sultan bin Saif, filled with rubble and ringed by 480 gun-ports
sites.sa: برج دائري ضخم بُني في خمسينيات القرن السابع عشر في عهد الإمام سلطان بن سيف، مملوء بالردم ومحاط بـ480 فتحة للبنادق
sites.desc: Nizwa Fort was built in the 1650s under Imam Sultan bin Saif, the second Ya'rubi ruler, over an underlying structure of the 12th century; the main work took about 12 years. The round tower is about 36 m in diameter and 30 m high (official tourism figures give 45 m and 34 m), its foundations go about 30 m into the ground, and part of it is filled with rocks, dirt and rubble above an underground stream. Defences include murder holes above the doors, about 24 openings for mortar fire, 480 gun-ports, 24 original cannons of which four remain, pitfalls in the twisting stair and cellars for food and munitions. One cannon from Boston was presented to the first Omani ambassador to the United States in 1840.
sites.sig: It is the best-known of Oman's forts and the seat from which the Ya'ariba imams ruled the interior.
sites.ex: Built under Imam Sultan bin Saif al-Ya’rubi; managed as a heritage site by Oman (Omran)

sites.s: Painted-ceiling palace of Imam Bilarab bin Sultan · Bahla
sites.se: A five-storey palace of plastered sandstone built in 1670 by Imam Bilarab bin Sultan, famed for ceilings painted with calligraphy and a Sun and Moon room with 14 windows
sites.sa: قصر من خمسة طوابق من الحجر الرملي المُجصّص بناه الإمام بلعرب بن سلطان عام 1670، يشتهر بسقوفه المزخرفة بالخط العربي وبغرفة الشمس والقمر ذات الـ14 نافذة
sites.desc: Jabrin Castle stands among farms in the Wilayat of Bahla, Al Dakhiliyah. It was built in 1670 by Imam Bilarab bin Sultan bin Saif al-Ya'rubi, third of the Ya'ariba imams, from grey sandstone covered in thick plaster, with five floors and 55 rooms around two courtyards 16 and 22 m high, each with a well more than 20 m deep. Many rooms have ceilings painted with Arabic calligraphy; the Sun and Moon room has 14 windows, the upper ones admitting moonlight and the lower controlling daylight, and the imam's protection room contains four secret trenches. Two towers defended it, a falaj waters the orchards, and it served first as the imam's palace and later as a seat of government; it also held a library, a courtroom and a classroom for Quran lessons, and the imam was buried in a corner of the ground floor.
sites.sig: It is the finest example of Omani palace decoration from the Ya'ariba period.
sites.ex: Built under Imam Bilarab bin Sultan; open daily as a heritage site

sites.s: 5 km karst cave with an underground lake and blind fish · show cave since 2006
sites.p: Karst in Cretaceous limestone of the Hajar
sites.se: A 5 km cave at the foot of Jebel Shams, believed to be 2 million years old, whose lake is home to the Omani blind cave fish
sites.sa: كهف بطول 5 كم عند سفح جبل شمس يُعتقد أن عمره مليونا سنة، تعيش في بحيرته سمكة الكهف العُمانية العمياء
sites.desc: Al Hoota Cave lies at Al Hamra in Ad Dakhiliyah at the foot of Jebel Shams. The karst system is about 5 km long, of which 4.5 km is show cave, with its highest point about 65 m above the entrance; it is believed to be about two million years old and opened to visitors in 2006 with electric lighting and a guided walk of 500 m ending at an underground lake 800 m long. The lake holds the Omani blind cave fish (Garra barreimiae), whose adults lose their eyesight, and the cave shelters more than 100 animal species including bats, hunter spiders and water beetles. Its stalagmites have been used for palaeoclimate research, including a 2022 Science study on droughts in late antique Arabia.
sites.sig: It is Oman's only developed show cave and a natural archive of past climate.
sites.ex: Managed as a show cave (opened 2006); stalagmites studied by D. Fleitmann et al.

sites.s: Collapse sinkhole in coastal limestone · Hawiyat Najm Park
sites.el: About 50 by 70 m wide and 20 m deep
sites.te: The well of the falling star
sites.se: A sinkhole 50 by 70 m across and 20 m deep, 600 m from the sea, formed when the roof of dissolved limestone collapsed; locals once blamed a meteorite
sites.sa: بلعة بعرض 50 في 70 م وعمق 20 م على بعد 600 م من البحر، تكوّنت عندما انهار سقف الحجر الجيري المذاب؛ وكان الأهالي يعزونها إلى نيزك
sites.desc: Hawiyat Najm, 'the deep well of the falling star', lies between Dibab and Bimmah on the Muscat–Sur highway, about 600 m from the sea. The sinkhole is roughly 50 m by 70 m across and about 20 m deep, and formed when the surface layer collapsed as the underlying limestone dissolved. The name records a local belief that a meteorite made it. The municipality has developed Hawiyat Najm Park around it, fenced, with a stairway down to the water.
sites.sig: It is the most accessible example of karst collapse on Oman's eastern coast.

sites.s: Wind-sculpted limestone and sandstone about 40 million years old · Al Wusta
sites.se: Six square kilometres of limestone and sandstone laid down some 40 million years ago and eroded by wind and water into statue-like forms
sites.sa: ستة كيلومترات مربعة من الحجر الجيري والرملي ترسّبت قبل نحو 40 مليون سنة ونحتتها الرياح والمياه في أشكال تشبه التماثيل
sites.desc: The Rock Garden lies in the centre of Duqm, about 550 km from Muscat, inside the Special Economic Zone at Duqm. It covers about 6 km² of sandstone and limestone in which fragile limestone deposits, formed roughly 40 million years ago, are capped by a harder layer; wind and water erosion over millions of years sculpted them into symmetrical, statue-like forms. The site is fenced with visitor gates, parking and surveillance cameras and is run by the zone authority's Technical Affairs Department, which in 2024 commissioned a study for walkways and lighting. Admission is free.
sites.sig: It is described as one of the most important geological sites in Oman.

sites.s: Drowned valley of the sinking Musandam peninsula · 16 km long
sites.p: Jurassic Musandam Group limestone, drowned by Neogene subsidence
sites.dr: Collision began about 5 million years ago
sites.el: Peninsula sinking about 6 mm a year
sites.se: A 16 km inlet walled by 800 m cliffs, a river valley drowned as the Arabian plate bends down under Eurasia at 6 mm a year
sites.sa: خور بطول 16 كم تحيط به جروف بارتفاع 800 م، وادٍ نهري غمره البحر مع انثناء الصفيحة العربية تحت الصفيحة الأوراسية بمعدل 6 مم في السنة
sites.desc: Khor Ash Sham is the longest of the Musandam inlets, about 16 km long with walls rising about 800 m from the water. The inlets are rias, drowned river valleys that resemble fjords but were never carved by ice, since no glaciers have covered the Arabian Peninsula since the Permian; the peninsula is subsiding at about 6 mm a year as the Arabian lithosphere is flexed down beneath the Eurasian plate, in a collision that began about 5 million years ago. The cliffs are Jurassic Musandam Group carbonates about 1,500 m thick, with the Upper Triassic Ghalilah Formation exposed at sea level, and the Hagab Thrust records about 15 km of shortening. Telegraph Island in the inlet carries the foundations of a British cable repeater station built in 1865 and abandoned in 1868, and the khor has a healthy dolphin population.
sites.sig: It is the clearest place in Arabia to see a continent being pulled down into a plate collision.

sites.s: Oman Exotic limestone block with a 1,000 m south face · Wadi al-Ayn
sites.p: Permian–Triassic Oman Exotic limestone, thrust onto Arabia in the Late Cretaceous
sites.te: A reef that sank, then rose
sites.se: A 2,090 m comb-shaped mountain of exotic limestone, a sunken reef platform carried onto Arabia when the Tethys closed, with a near-vertical face over 1,000 m
sites.sa: جبل على شكل مشط بارتفاع 2,090 م من الحجر الجيري الدخيل، منصة شعابية غارقة حُملت على شبه الجزيرة العربية عند انغلاق محيط تيثس، بواجهة شبه عمودية تتجاوز 1,000 م
sites.desc: Jebel Misht, 'Comb Mountain', rises to 2,090 m above Wadi al-Ayn about 50 km north-west of Nizwa, with a south face of over 1,000 m rising almost vertically. It is made of Oman Exotic Limestone, a block out of sequence with the surrounding rocks that was thrust onto Arabia when the Tethys Ocean closed about 65 million years ago. The Oman Exotics are limestones caught up in the thrust stack beneath the Semail Ophiolite; the Middle–Late Permian ones were reef build-ups on platforms that sank to ocean depths during rifting and were later engulfed by basalts, and carry foraminifera, calcareous algae, corals and crinoids. Michael Searle, Peter King and Philip Davis made the first recorded ascent by the west ridge on 11–12 February 1982, and the south face was climbed in February 1983.
sites.sig: It is the most dramatic of Oman's exotic blocks, a piece of Tethyan sea floor standing on the desert edge.
sites.ex: Geology by M. P. Searle; Permian exotics studied by O. Abdelghany, A. R. Fowler & W. Hashem (2019)
disc: Exotic limestone out of sequence with its surroundings

sites.s: Largest shorebird wetland in the Middle East · Ramsar site 2529
sites.te: Half a million birds on the mud
sites.se: A 2,137 km² peninsula of mudflats, seagrass and reef on the Arabian Sea where up to half a million waterbirds from Arctic Russia and Central Asia winter
sites.sa: شبه جزيرة بمساحة 2,137 كم² من المسطحات الطينية والأعشاب البحرية والشعاب على بحر العرب، يشتو فيها حتى نصف مليون طائر مائي قادم من روسيا القطبية وآسيا الوسطى
sites.desc: Barr Al Hikman in Mahout, Al Wusta, about 400 km south of Muscat, was made a nature reserve by Royal Decree 51/2014 and designated Ramsar site 2529 on 25 October 2023 with an area of 213,715 ha. A January 2016 count recorded 464,887 waterbirds, including 125,659 dunlin, 123,369 lesser sandplover and 60,976 bar-tailed godwit, and 18 species exceed 1% of their flyway populations; it is described as the most significant wintering wetland in the Middle East. Its Halodule and Halophila seagrass beds are the largest in Oman, with about 1,500 ha of coral reef and 200 ha of Avicennia mangrove, and the waters are used by the endangered Arabian Sea humpback whale and green and hawksbill turtles. Ten years of surveys by Wetlands International with Radboud University, Groningen, NIOZ and Sultan Qaboos University produced the 2018 book 'Barr Al Hikman: shorebird paradise in Oman'.
sites.sig: It is the single most important stop on the West Asian–East African flyway for Arctic-breeding shorebirds.

sites.s: Grey-mangrove reserve inside Muscat · Ramsar site 2144
sites.p: Avicennia marina mangrove and tidal creek
sites.se: About 172 ha of grey mangrove in the heart of Muscat, protected since 1975, with 194 bird, 40 fish, 27 crustacean and 48 mollusc species
sites.sa: نحو 172 هكتاراً من أشجار القرم الرمادي في قلب مسقط، محمية منذ 1975، تضم 194 نوعاً من الطيور و40 من الأسماك و27 من القشريات و48 من الرخويات
sites.desc: Qurm Nature Reserve lies within the urban area of Qurm in Bawshar, Muscat, on the Sea of Oman, and takes its name from the grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) that dominates it. It was established in 1975 by decree of Sultan Qaboos, recognised as an Important Bird Area in 1994, and its lower 106.8 ha were designated Ramsar site 2144 on 19 April 2013; the whole reserve covers about 172 ha. The Ramsar record lists 194 bird species, more than 40 fish species including commercial ones, 27 crustaceans and 48 molluscs, and calls it one of the largest mangrove areas on the east coast of the Arabian Peninsula. It is being developed as a conservation and education site with a visitor centre.
sites.sig: It is the largest natural mangrove stand on Oman's northern coast and a nursery for the capital's fisheries.

sites.s: Arabian tahr stronghold in the Eastern Hajar · UNESCO biosphere reserve 2025
sites.te: The shy goat of the cliffs
sites.se: A 1,039 km² mountain reserve 45 km south-west of Muscat set up in 1975 for the Arabian tahr, with 400 plant species, ten of them endemic
sites.sa: محمية جبلية بمساحة 1,039 كم² على بعد 45 كم جنوب غرب مسقط أُنشئت عام 1975 للطهر العربي، فيها 400 نوع نباتي عشرة منها متوطنة
sites.desc: Al Sireen Nature Reserve was set up in 1975 in the Eastern Hajar about 45 km south-west of Muscat, bordering the wilayats of Al Amerat, Qurayat and Dima wa Tayeen, with entry points at Jabal Aswad and Jabal Abyad. It covers 103,888 ha and is an IUCN Category II protected area. Its flagship species is the Arabian tahr, the smallest of the ibex-like goats, which hides among large rocks, can go two or three days without drinking and is threatened by poaching and urban expansion; Arabian gazelle, Arabian wolf, red fox, Egyptian vulture and the Oman saw-scaled viper also live there, with about 400 plant species including ten endemic and four endangered. In September 2025 UNESCO's MAB council added it, with Al Jabal al Akhdar, to the World Network of Biosphere Reserves, Oman's first; about 2,533 people live in its buffer zone.
sites.sig: It is the main protected refuge of the endangered Arabian tahr, found only in the Hajar mountains.

sites.s: Nine coastal lagoons protected since 1997 · Dhofar
sites.p: Brackish coastal lagoons with reed and mangrove
sites.se: A chain of nine brackish lagoons along the Dhofar coast, from Mughsayl to Khawr Rori, where migrants from Africa, Europe and India rest among reeds and mangroves
sites.sa: سلسلة من تسعة أخوار قليلة الملوحة على ساحل ظفار من المغسيل إلى خور روري، تستريح فيها الطيور المهاجرة من أفريقيا وأوروبا والهند بين القصب وأشجار القرم
sites.desc: The Dhofar government's protected region covers nine wetlands: Khawr Mughsayl, Khawr Dahareez, Khawr Baleed, Khawr Awqad, Khawr Sawli, Khawr Taqah, Khawr Rawri, Khawr Qurm al Sagheer and Khawr Qurm al Kabeer, declared protected in June 1997. They range from a few hectares to more than a hundred: Khawr Mughsayl is about 3 km long and 150 m wide, Khawr Awqad about 16 ha and Khawr Taqah about 2 km². More than 160 bird species have been recorded, the lagoons being important stopovers for migrants, with milkfish and mullet that tolerate changing salinity, reed-mace (Typha) and mangroves, which are being planted to give cover for birds. The management plan allows controlled fodder cutting and limited visitor facilities and protects the archaeological sites beside them.
sites.sig: Together the khawrs are the main freshwater-influenced bird habitat on Oman's monsoon coast.

sites.n: Hallaniyat Bay and the Arabian Sea humpback whale
sites.na: خليج الحلانيات والحوت الأحدب في بحر العرب
sites.s: Only non-migrating humpback population, fewer than 100 whales · Dhofar
sites.se: A tiny, isolated humpback population off Dhofar and the Gulf of Masirah that breeds and feeds in the same waters year-round and is now proposed as a fourth subspecies
sites.sa: مجموعة صغيرة معزولة من الحيتان الحدباء قبالة ظفار وخليج مصيرة تتكاثر وتتغذى في المياه نفسها طوال العام، ويُقترح الآن اعتبارها نويعاً رابعاً
sites.desc: The Oman Arabian Sea Important Marine Mammal Area covers 96,146 km² and holds the Arabian Sea humpback whale, estimated by mark-recapture at 82 individuals (95% CI 60–111) from 2000–2004 photo-identification, the basis of its IUCN Endangered listing. Satellite tags on 14 whales in 2014–2015 showed strong fidelity to two hotspots, Dhofar (Hallaniyat Bay), linked to reproduction, and the Gulf of Masirah, linked to feeding; at least 20 cetacean species use the area, including blue, Bryde's and sperm whales. Unlike other humpbacks they do not migrate. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Marine Science led by the Wildlife Conservation Society and the Environment Society of Oman, analysing mitochondrial DNA from 2,285 whales, found the population diverged 43,000–113,000 years ago, has the lowest genetic diversity of any humpback region and merits recognition as a fourth subspecies; threats include fishing-gear entanglement, vessel strikes and noise.
sites.sig: It is the world's only resident, non-migratory humpback whale population, and one of its smallest.
sites.ex: Environment Society of Oman; Wildlife Conservation Society; IUCN Marine Mammal Protected Areas Task Force

sites.s: Acacia woodland and Arabian gazelle herds · Al Kamil wal Wafi
sites.p: Samr (Acacia tortilis) savanna on gravel plain
sites.se: A 220 km² acacia plain in Sharqiyah, protected in 1997, where Arabian gazelle herds have recovered from over-hunting among 57 bird and 166 insect species
sites.sa: سهل من السمر بمساحة 220 كم² في الشرقية حُمي عام 1997، تعافت فيه قطعان الغزال العربي من الصيد الجائر وسط 57 نوعاً من الطيور و166 من الحشرات
sites.desc: Al Saleel Natural Park lies at Al Kamil wal Wafi in Ash Sharqiyah, bounded by a mountain range to the north, a plain reaching the Gehwan reserve to the east and Wadi Al Bathaa and the Sharqiya Sands to the south. Set up in 1997, it covers 220 km² predominantly forested with samr (umbrella thorn acacia) and salam (Acacia ehrenbergiana) among more than 100 plant species. Its Arabian gazelle, once sharply reduced by over-hunting, are now seen in large herds thanks to local cooperation against poaching; the reserve also records about 57 bird species including steppe eagle, Arabian ibex, red fox, Cape hare, eight reptiles and 166 insect species, and the Omani wild cat is listed among its rare species. Visitors need a permit from the Environment Authority.

sites.n: Al Jabal Al Akhdar and the Saiq Plateau
sites.s: Terraced rose gardens at 2,000 m · UNESCO biosphere reserve 2025
sites.se: A high limestone plateau where falaj-fed terraces grow roses for rosewater, pomegranates and walnuts, home to wild olive, Arabian ibex and 71 bird species
sites.sa: هضبة جيرية عالية تروي أفلاجها مدرّجات الورد لصناعة ماء الورد والرمان والجوز، وتعيش فيها الزيتون البري والوعل العربي و71 نوعاً من الطيور
sites.desc: Al Jabal Al Akhdar in Ad Dakhiliyah is a mostly limestone massif about 150 km from Muscat whose Saiq plateau lies at about 2,000 m. Its mild, Mediterranean-type climate and mountain springs feed falaj channels and a centuries-old terrace system that grows roses for traditional rosewater, pomegranates, walnuts, apricots, grapes and peaches, and it is a major area for honey-bee breeding; rock-art figures about 6,000 years old have been studied on the mountain. In August 2011 a decree created the Jebel Akhdar Sanctuary for Natural Sceneries, and in September 2025 UNESCO's MAB council listed the Al Jabal al Akhdar Landscape, about 4,500 ha, as a biosphere reserve for its rare wild olive trees, threatened Arabian ibex and Arabian wolf and more than 71 bird species including Egyptian vulture and golden eagle.
sites.sig: It is Oman's highland agricultural heartland and, with Al Sireen, its first UNESCO biosphere reserve.

sites.desc: Al Khoud in Wilayat As Seeb is one of the 30 Muscat geosites in the Ministry of Tourism's Muscat Geoheritage guide launched in 2012. Here the siliciclastic Al-Khod Formation, of Campanian(?) to Maastrichtian(?) age, was deposited nonconformably on the Semail Ophiolite. Above an angular unconformity, shallow-marine limestones of Paleocene to Miocene age follow, including the Seeb Formation, whose basal unit is about 20–40 m of lagoonal packstones and grainstones dated by foraminifera to the middle Eocene. Dinosaur footprints, bones and fossil dung about 70 million years old have been reported from the Al Khoudh area by Sultan Qaboos University geologists and the Oman Geological Society.

A large permanent brackish lagoon with about 1 m of organic mud sits behind a sand barrier about 4 m high, within late Holocene deposits. sites.desc: A karst sinkhole on the Qara plateau between Salalah and Mirbat, with an oval opening of about 130 × 90 m at about 680 m above sea level and a shaft about 210 m deep that narrows to about 60 m across at 100 m depth. A long wadi ends at the shaft, making it a river sink, and the groundwater table lies at its base. In 1980 British cavers collected a depigmented cyprinid fish from a pool in a side passage about 200 m down; it was described in 1987 as Garra dunsirei, known only from this sinkhole. The species is assessed as Endangered by IUCN (2015). The shaft was explored in 1997 by Slovenian cavers and members of Sultan Qaboos University.

sites.desc: A large doline on the karst plateau of the Qara Mountains, Dhofar, about 1,000 m long east–west and about 500 m wide, with a vertical range of 250 m. Its floor lies at about 740 m above sea level, below surrounding hills that exceed 1,000 m. It sits where two large wadis meet, and its floor has numerous swallow holes that drain water underground after rare heavy rains. The official explanation is the collapse of a huge underground chamber; other proposed factors include repeated collapses, widening by wadi water and higher groundwater in a wetter past. sites.te: Springs that turn air into stone
sites.se: In Wadi Mahram, water from deep mantle rock is so alkaline that it pulls carbon dioxide from the air and turns it into white stone

sites.desc: Hyperalkaline springs emerge from the peridotite (mantle) section of the Samail ophiolite at Falaij and in neighbouring Wadi Mahram, in the Wilayat of Samail. Outlet water at Falaij measured pH 11.52–11.63 and 27.9–30.8 °C, and recent travertine was sampled in Wadi Mahram. Such waters react with atmospheric CO2 to precipitate carbonate; across the Oman springs, fresh precipitates date from modern to 350 years and travertine terraces to about 45,000 years. Terraces are typically about 200,000 m² in area and about 1 m thick, growing at about 0.1–0.3 mm per year.

sites.s: Mantle rock turned completely to carbonate along the ophiolite’s basal thrust
sites.se: Near Fanja, bands of rock that were once mantle peridotite became fully carbonate, locking away huge amounts of CO2
sites.sa: قرب فنجاء تحوّلت أشرطة من صخور كانت يومًا من بيريدوتيت الوشاح إلى كربونات بالكامل، فاختزنت كميات هائلة من ثاني أكسيد الكربون
sites.desc: On a ridge crest just north of Wadi Mansah, about 12 km south-east of Fanjah, peridotite near the base of the Samail ophiolite has been completely carbonated to listvenite (magnesite/dolomite plus quartz). The listvenite bands are about 10 to 200 m thick and run roughly parallel to the banding of the host peridotite along the ophiolite’s basal thrust. Mineral assemblages indicate formation at about 80–130 °C, and clumped isotope thermometry gives about 90 ± 15 °C. An internal Rb–Sr isochron gives 97 ± 29 Ma, linking carbonation to ophiolite emplacement.
sites.sig: Shows that peridotite can be fully carbonated in nature, a key analogue for permanent CO2 storage.

sites.s: Vast inland sabkha at the edge of the Rub’ al Khali · the Mother of Poisons
sites.dr: Deflation basin formed before 30 ka; arid gypsum/halite crusts since 5.5 ka

sites.se: A shining salt flat where the mountains’ water ends its journey, its thin crust hiding treacherous mud

sites.desc: Umm al Samim is an inland sabkha and groundwater sump of about 3,000 km² at about 55 m elevation, at the south-western foot of the Oman Mountains on the eastern edge of the Rub’ al Khali. It is fed by dune sand, alluvium from the mountains and groundwater from Tertiary Umm Er Radhuma limestone aquifers. The closed depression formed by wind deflation in the gypsiferous Fars Group before 30,000 years ago and has since alternated between saline lake and sabkha phases, with arid capillary gypsum and halite forming since about 5,500 years ago. Its fragile crust over wet sediment earned it the names Mother of Poisons and Mother of Worries; Wilfred Thesiger was the first European to see it, in the late 1940s.
sites.sig: The largest inland sabkha of the Oman foreland, recording desert climate change over the last 30,000 years.

sites.desc: Lasail, inland of Sohar in North Al Batinah, is a massive sulphide copper deposit within the Samail ophiolite and an underground mine operated by Oman Mining Company. Its ore and stockwork zones contain chalcopyrite, bornite, cubanite, pyrite, pyrrhotite and sphalerite, with magnetite, hematite, quartz and traces of gold. Studies of the Lasail and nearby Bayda deposits describe hydrothermal mineralisation and alteration of the host basalt in stockwork zones beneath the sulphide bodies. Copper exports from Lasail resumed in 2025 after about 30 years.

sites.se: Rocks in the Huqf desert record a strange global upheaval in ocean chemistry just before the first animals spread
sites.sa: تسجّل صخور صحراء الحقف اضطرابًا عالميًا غريبًا في كيمياء المحيطات قُبيل انتشار الحيوانات الأولى
sites.desc: Wadi Shuram in the Huqf area of central Oman exposes the Ediacaran Shuram Formation, the eponym of the Shuram carbon-isotope excursion, in which carbonate δ13C falls abruptly to about −12‰ worldwide. Measured sections in the wadi were logged with GPS waypoints by Bergmann (2013), including a section of 217 m. Radiometric calibration places the onset in Oman after 578.2 ± 5.9 Ma and its end by 562.7 ± 3.8 Ma, a span of less than 15.5 ± 7.0 million years. The excursion coincides with key steps in the early evolution of animals.

sites.desc: Wadi Gideah, in the Wadi Tayin massif of the Samail ophiolite near Ibra, exposes a near-continuous section through about 6,500 m of fossil oceanic crust formed at a fast-spreading ridge. The data show systematic, contrasting compositional trends in the lower and upper gabbros that correlate with stratigraphic depth. The section is used as an on-land analogue and reference for fast-spread lower oceanic crust.

The Musandam mountains are built of a stable-platform succession about 4 km thick, mostly carbonates, deposited from the Permian to the Early Cretaceous, including about 1,500 m of Jurassic Musandam Group carbonates. Today the Arabian plate here is flexed northward beneath Eurasia and subsides by about 6 mm per year, drowning the peninsula’s valleys into fjord-like inlets.

sites.desc: A small island in Khor Ash Sham (Elphinstone Inlet), about 160 m long and up to 90 m wide, where a repeater station on the London–Karachi telegraph cable was built in 1864; the Musandam–Bushire section was completed on 25 March 1864. Siemens supplied the equipment and operators’ quarters were built on the island. Extreme heat and isolation made the posting notoriously hard, and the station was abandoned in December 1868 when the cable was diverted to Henjam and Jask. The ruins are now visited by dhow tours and a tourism development project is under way.

Jazirat Umm al Fayyarin is the most important seabird breeding island in the region, with terns nesting in significant numbers. sites.sa: تحيط المزارع بحصن لوى ذي الأبراج الخمسة، وقد كان مقرًّا للوالي وأسرته
sites.desc: Liwa Fort in North Al Batinah was built by the Ya’rubids about 400 years ago, under Imam Nasir bin Murshid or Sultan bin Saif. It measures 58 m by 75 m, with high walls, five observation towers and a three-storey central building, Al-Qasbah, that housed the Wali’s family. It served as a defensive structure, the Wali’s residence and the seat of the province’s affairs, and was garrisoned by the army until 2002. Restoration began in 2000 and was completed in 2003, and the fort is open to the public.
sites.sig: A typical Ya’rubi coastal-plain fort that remained an administrative centre into modern times.

sites.s: Historic quarter of the Buraimi Oasis with a rare moated fort
sites.dr: Hamasa over 500 years old; Al Khandaq Fort built by Mutlaq al-Mutayri (r. 1808–13), restored 1994 and 2015–2018
sites.el: Fort ringed by a dry moat
sites.se: In the old Buraimi Oasis, a fort hides behind a deep ditch, a rare defence in Oman
sites.sa: في واحة البريمي القديمة يتحصّن حصن خلف خندق عميق، وهو دفاع نادر في عُمان
sites.desc: Hamasa is a historic quarter of the Buraimi Oasis on the Oman–UAE border, described by the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism as over 500 years old and linked by Falaj Al Jaimi. Al Khandaq Fort stands here, square in plan with four round towers and named after the dry moat that surrounds it, a feature rare in Omani fortification. The Buraimi Oasis Landscape Archaeology Project attributes the fort to Mutlaq al-Mutayri (r. 1808–13) and also recorded Iron Age mounds, aflaj and Late Islamic settlements across the oasis. The fort was restored in 1994 and again between 2015 and 2018.
sites.sig: A rare moated fort at the heart of one of south-east Arabia’s oldest oasis landscapes.

sites.n: Al Hajar Geopark (aspiring UNESCO Global Geopark)
sites.s: Oman’s first national geopark project · about 5,400 km² across 11 wilayats
sites.dr: Aspiring UNESCO Global Geopark; dossier submitted to UNESCO September 2026
sites.el: About 5,400 km² in 3 governorates and 11 wilayats
sites.te: A whole mountain range as a museum
sites.se: Across 11 wilayats of the Hajar Mountains, Oman is turning fossil corals, springs, aflaj and old villages into one great geopark
sites.sa: في إحدى عشرة ولاية من جبال الحجر تجمع عُمان المرجان الأحفوري والعيون والأفلاج والقرى القديمة في جيوبارك واحد كبير
sites.desc: Al Hajar Geopark is described by the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism as Oman’s first national geopark project, covering about 5,400 km² in 11 wilayats of Al Dakhiliyah, South Al Batinah and North Al Sharqiyah governorates. Its themes are geological and natural heritage, tangible and intangible cultural heritage, water resources and biological resources. The official map numbers 22 sites, among them Hasat Bin Salt, Ar Rustaq Fort, the Ayn Al Kasfah and Ayn Ath Thowwarah springs, the aflaj Al Muyassar, Al Malki, Al Khatmeen and Daris, and the Coral Garden and Fish Fossils of Al Jabal Al Akhdar. The booklet dates the Coral Garden corals to the late Permian, about 250 million years ago.
sites.sig: Oman’s bid to have the geology, water systems and mountain villages of the central Hajar recognised together as a UNESCO Global Geopark.

sites.s: Mountain reserve of over 860 km² · Arabian tahr and wintering houbara
sites.se: In the mountains of Al Dhahirah, Arabian tahr climb the cliffs while houbara bustards spend the winter on the plains of Al Mazem
sites.sa: في جبال الظاهرة يتسلّق الطهر العربي المنحدرات، وتقضي طيور الحبارى الشتاء في سهول المازم
sites.desc: Al Dhahirah Natural Reserve was established by Royal Decree 24/2024, issued on 8 April 2024, with its areas set out in an annex and map. According to the Environment Authority, it covers more than 860 km² of a mountain range in Al Dhahirah Governorate, running from south of Wadi Al Fath in the Wilayat of Yanqul to the Al Mazem area north-west of Ibri, and extending south-west towards the Empty Quarter. More than 70 wild plant species are recorded, with the Arabian tahr, lynx, mountain fox, wild rabbit, wild cat, wild birds and the Omani lizard. Al Mazem is an important winter habitat for the houbara bustard.
sites.sig: Protects a long mountain range of north-western Oman that shelters the endangered Arabian tahr.

sites.s: Great Ya’ariba fortress at the foot of the Hajar · UNESCO Tentative List
sites.dr: Built about 1250 AD; rebuilt under the Ya’ariba 1624–1649; UNESCO Tentative List 1988
sites.el: Four towers; the Devils Tower about 18.5 m high
sites.se: At the edge of the Batinah plain, Rostaq Fort rises with four great towers, one of them holding the tomb of an imam
sites.sa: عند طرف سهل الباطنة ترتفع قلعة الرستاق بأبراجها الأربعة الكبيرة، وفي أحدها قبر إمام
sites.desc: Rostaq Fort stands on the slopes of Al Jabal Al Akhdar at the edge of the Batinah plain in South Al Batinah Governorate. It was first built around 1250 AD and rebuilt by the first imams of the Ya’ariba dynasty between 1624 and 1649. It has a ground floor and two upper floors with residences, weapon stores, reception halls, a mosque, prisons and wells, and four towers: the Red Tower, the Wind Tower, the Devils Tower and the Modern Tower. It is a component of ‘The forts of Rostaq and al-Hazm’ on Oman’s UNESCO Tentative List and site no. 2 on the Al Hajar Geopark map.
sites.sig: One of Oman’s largest historic forts and a seat of the Ya’ariba imams.

sites.s: Seafront castle above Mirbat’s old port and market · seat of the wali
sites.dr: A castle at Mirbat was recorded in 1884; rebuilt under Sultan Said bin Taimur
sites.el: Rectangular plan with two defensive towers, two floors
sites.te: The castle above the old harbour
sites.se: On the eastern edge of Mirbat, a two-tower castle looks down on the old port and the traditional market
sites.sa: على الطرف الشرقي من مرباط يطلّ حصن ذو برجين على الميناء القديم والسوق التقليدي
sites.desc: A castle on the eastern side of Mirbat, Dhofar, overlooking the old seaport (al-Furda) and the traditional Mirbat market. The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism notes that no precise date for the original building is known; the British writer Miles reported a castle there after visiting Mirbat in 1884, and the present building was rebuilt during the reign of Sultan Said bin Taimur. It has a rectangular plan with two main entrances and two defensive towers on two floors: the ground floor held servants’ rooms, soldiers’ quarters, an arms store, a prison and a kitchen, and the upper floor four residential rooms including a majlis for the wali’s family. It is open to visitors.
sites.sig: The administrative and defensive heart of historic Mirbat, one of Dhofar’s old trading ports.

sites.s: Early 20th-century residence of Taqah’s sheikh and wali · now a museum
sites.dr: Built in the reign of Sultan Taimur bin Faisal (1913–1932); renovated 1991, museum from 1994
sites.te: The governor’s home by the sea
sites.se: In the fishing town of Taqah, a stone castle with three watchtowers shows how a Dhofari governor lived
sites.sa: في بلدة طاقة الساحلية يكشف حصن حجري بثلاثة أبراج مراقبة كيف كان يعيش والٍ في ظفار
sites.desc: A two-storey stone building in Taqah, Dhofar, built as the residence of Sheikh Ali bin Timman Al Ma’shani during the reign of Sultan Taimur bin Faisal (1913–1932). In the 1960s an outer wall and three defensive watchtowers were added to protect the wali, who used it as his private residence until 1984. The ground floor has a reception hall (barza), a guard room, a weapons store and a prison; the upper floor held the wali’s family quarters. It was renovated in 1991 and reopened as a museum in 1994.
sites.sig: A well-preserved example of a 20th-century Dhofari governor’s residence and administrative centre.

sites.conf: Coordinates from the Archnet map marker; about 1.9 km from the existing Salalah khawrs point but a separate historic building; Archnet’s style-period year 1744 is not explained and is not used

sites.s: Abandoned coastal village with shell midden and 200-tomb cemetery · eastern Dhofar
sites.dr: Surface pottery dates the ruins to the 17th century or later
sites.el: Village of about 3–5 ha; cemetery of about 200 tombs
sites.se: On a terrace above a silted wadi mouth, stone houses, a tiny mosque and a huge pile of shells mark an old fishing village
sites.sa: على مصطبة فوق مصبّ وادٍ طمرته الرواسب، تدلّ بيوت حجرية ومسجد صغير وكومة هائلة من الأصداف على قرية صيد قديمة
sites.desc: A coastal site about 200 km north-east of Salalah, on a terrace about 5 m above a small silted wadi estuary near Hasik. It comprises a village of roughly 3–5 ha with stone houses, single-room storehouses and a square mosque about 5 × 5 m with a mihrab in its west wall, a large shell midden, and a cemetery about 200 m to the north with roughly 200 tombs marked by plain upright stelae. Surface finds include iron tools, glass bangles, Bahla ware, blue-and-white porcelain, stoneware and green-glazed ware, which date the ruins to the 17th century or later. The site was surveyed by the University of Naples L’Orientale mission.
sites.sig: A rare recorded late Islamic fishing settlement on the remote eastern Dhofar coast.
refs: Giunta, R. & Pavan, A. (2022). First Archaeological Activities by the University of Naples L’Orientale in Dhofar, Sultanate of Oman. Archeologia tra Oriente e Occidente 1. https://unora.unior.it/bitstream/11574/216023/1/Giunta_Pavan%20First%20archaeological%20activities%202022.pdf
sites.conf: Coordinates are the published village point (17°23′53.1″N 55°17′22.5″E); the paper also lists 55°17′42.5″E for the village. The end of occupation is not dated, so t1 (about 1900) is a broad estimate. Arabic name: حاسك is established; القديمة translates ‘Qadim’

sites.s: Walled promontory settlement above Salalah’s port · pre-Islamic and medieval
sites.dr: Two occupation phases; few sherds suggest late pre-Islamic then medieval occupation
sites.el: Promontory site about 42 m wide and 75 m north–south
sites.se: High on a rocky cape west of Salalah, old stone walls once watched for fish, ships and enemies
sites.sa: على رأس صخري غرب صلالة كانت أسوار حجرية قديمة ترقب أسراب السمك والسفن والأعداء
sites.desc: A promontory site at Raysut, west of Salalah, overlooking the modern Salalah port and now enclosed by a modern wall; the surveyed area is about 42 m wide and 75 m north–south. Phillips (1972) described a defensive wall on the west and south sides and dwellings of semi-dressed stone on bedrock, similar to the older walls of Al Baleed. Brief excavations by the American Foundation for the Study of Man identified two occupation phases, and Newton and Zarins (2017) reported two cemeteries of boat-shaped graves and a fortified headland settlement comparable to Khor Rori. The few sherds collected in the 2022 survey suggest a late pre-Islamic occupation followed by a medieval one.
sites.sig: One of the fortified coastal sites of ancient Dhofar, linked by building technique to Al Baleed and Sumhuram.
refs: Giunta, R. & Pavan, A. (2022). First Archaeological Activities by the University of Naples L’Orientale in Dhofar, Sultanate of Oman. Archeologia tra Oriente e Occidente 1. https://unora.unior.it/bitstream/11574/216023/1/Giunta_Pavan%20First%20archaeological%20activities%202022.pdf
sites.conf: Coordinates are the published point (16°56′02.3″N 54°00′30.3″E). The site is not firmly dated; the timeline (about AD 200 to AD 1500) is a broad estimate for ‘late pre-Islamic then medieval’. Arabic name is a descriptive rendering (ريسوت is established)

sites.s: Monsoon-fed karst spring building mossy tufa cliffs · Jebel Qara near Taqah
sites.dr: Tufa deposits from intermittent karst springs; not dated
sites.el: Tufa walls with bulbous forms and stalactites
sites.se: Above Taqah, spring water rich in lime trickles down a cliff and slowly turns into new rock
sites.sa: فوق طاقة يتساقط ماء نبع غني بالكلس على جرف صخري ويتحوّل ببطء إلى صخر جديد
sites.desc: A waterfall at Khasur in the Taqah area of Dhofar, formed where intermittent, lime-rich karst springs emerge from the limestone of the Qara mountains. As the water flows over the cliff it deposits tufa, building walls with the typical bulbous forms of tufa and some stalactites. The walls stay wet and mossy, especially after the summer monsoon (khareef). The site is freely accessible.
sites.sig: An accessible example of the active tufa deposition that shapes Dhofar’s monsoon springs.
refs: Duckeck, J. Ayn Athum Waterfall (شلالات عين اثوم), Oman. Showcaves.com. https://showcaves.com/english/om/karst/AynAthum.html

sites.s: Tufa-walled gorge and plunge pool below the Qara escarpment · rimstone dams like Plitvice
sites.dr: Rimstone pools, tufa deposits and a tufa cave; not dated
sites.el: Gorge about 170 m long; reported discharge 42 l/s
sites.se: North of Salalah, spring water has built its own stone dams and walls along a 170 m gorge
sites.sa: شمال صلالة بنى ماء الينابيع سدوده وجدرانه الحجرية بنفسه على امتداد خانق طوله 170 مترًا
sites.desc: A spring site at the foot of the Qara hills north of Salalah, reached by following the valley upstream from Itin Street. Karst water feeds an intermittent wadi in which precipitated limestone forms dams and pools; when the river is dry the pools become terraces and the dams vertical tufa walls. A gorge about 170 m long with tufa walls on both sides leads to a waterfall with a plunge pool and a small tufa cave, and a second tufa waterfall at Ittin lies about 800 m upstream. One source reports a discharge of 42 l/s.
sites.sig: Shows how karst springs on the Dhofar escarpment build rimstone dams and tufa walls.

sites.s: Small solution cave under an old river conglomerate · Wadi Halfayn, Izki
sites.dr: Cave dissolved below a calcite-cemented conglomerate; formation has stopped
sites.el: Triangular passage with flat ceiling and V-shaped walls
sites.te: The cave under the river stones
sites.se: Below the ruins of Al Nazar near Izki, a short cave hides under a roof made of old river pebbles
sites.sa: تحت أطلال قرية النزار قرب إزكي يختبئ كهف قصير تحت سقف من حصى نهر قديم
sites.desc: A small horizontal karst cave in Wilayat Izki, Ad Dakhiliyah, below the ruins of Al Nazar village in the normally dry Wadi Halfayn. It is cut in soft, fine-grained white limestone; its nearly horizontal ceiling is a conglomerate of rounded rubble cemented by calcite and capped by clay. The single, fairly straight passage has a triangular profile with a flat ceiling and V-shaped walls and ends after a few metres. Showcaves.com interprets it as dissolution of the limestone after the wadi cut deeper and drained the groundwater below the conglomerate; cave formation has since stopped. The name Jarnan is given as the pre-Islamic name of Izki.
sites.sig: A compact record of river erosion, cementation and later dissolution in the interior foothills.
refs: Duckeck, J. Jarnan Cave (كهف جرنان), Oman. Showcaves.com. https://showcaves.com/english/om/caves/Jarnan.html
sites.conf: Coordinates from Showcaves.com; the formation history is the page author’s interpretation; timeline is a broad Quaternary estimate because the cave is not dated

sites.s: Limestone gorge with turquoise pools and a waterfall inside a cave · near Tiwi
sites.dr: Gorge cut by flash floods; cave waterfall formed by fallen blocks
sites.te: The secret waterfall in the cave
sites.se: Walk and swim up a gorge of pale cliffs to find a waterfall hidden inside a cave
sites.sa: امشِ واسبح في خانق بين جروف شاحبة لتصل إلى شلال يختبئ داخل كهف
sites.desc: A gorge in the Ash Sharqiyah South Governorate, entered from the coast near Tiwi village about 170 km from Muscat. Sculpted limestone cliffs enclose a chain of clear turquoise pools, and the gorge is deepened by floodwater after heavy rain. About 45 minutes’ walk upstream, visitors swim through a narrow opening to a waterfall inside a cave, formed where rocks fell from the walls above. Access begins with a short boat crossing at the wadi mouth.
sites.sig: One of the best-known limestone gorges of the eastern Hajar coast.

sites.s: Window into Oman’s oldest crust · Tonian arc rocks about 880–830 million years old
sites.dr: Gneiss protolith 884 ± 4 Ma; granodiorite 836 ± 4 Ma; cooling about 830 Ma
sites.te: The oldest rocks of the east
sites.se: South of Sur, granite and gneiss show a slice of crust made in a volcanic arc almost 900 million years ago
sites.sa: جنوب صور تكشف صخور الجرانيت والنايس شريحة من قشرة تكوّنت في قوس بركاني قبل نحو 900 مليون عام
sites.desc: Jebel Ja’alan, about 50 km south of Sur and 15 km north of Jalan Bani Bu Ali, exposes Precambrian basement mapped over an area of about 2 × 3.5 km. Ten rock units were mapped, including the Al Wafi Schist, Ja’alan Gneiss, Ja’alan Granite and Kamil Granodiorite, cut by dolerite and andesite dykes. Zircon U–Pb dating gave 884 ± 4 Ma for the gneiss protolith and 836 ± 4 Ma for the granodiorite, with monazite in the schist recording metamorphism at 834 ± 12 Ma and muscovite cooling at about 830 Ma. Peak conditions of about 650–700 °C at 4–7.5 kbar and juvenile isotope signatures point to a volcanic-arc setting.
sites.sig: Among the oldest dated rocks in Oman, possibly the leading edge of India’s Neoproterozoic accretionary margin.
refs: Alessio, B.L., Blades, M.L., Murray, G., Thorpe, B., Collins, A.S., Kelsey, D.E., Foden, J., Payne, J., Al-Khirbash, S. & Jourdan, F. (2017). Origin and tectonic evolution of the NE basement of Oman: a window into the Neoproterozoic accretionary growth of India? Geological Magazine. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0016756817000061
sites.conf: Coordinates converted from published sample JA15-08 (UTM 40N, 742899 E, 2460099 N, WGS84); journal name inferred from the DOI. About 2 km from the existing Jabal Qahwan Nature Reserve point, which is an ecology record; this record covers the basement geology

sites.s: Four-towered 17th-century fort on a plateau above Sur
sites.dr: Attributed to Imam Nasir bin Murshid Al-Ya’rubi (first half of 17th century) or to the Portuguese; taken by Omanis in 1648; restored 1989
sites.el: About 2,500 m², walls about 55 m long and over 5 m high
sites.se: From a rocky plateau, Sunaysilah’s round and square towers once watched the coast and the road into Sur
sites.sa: من فوق هضبة صخرية كانت أبراج السنيسلة المستديرة والمربعة ترقب الساحل والطريق إلى صور
sites.desc: A fort on a high rocky plateau south of the village of Sunaysilah in Sur, Ash Sharqiyah South. The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism reports two accounts of its origin: construction ordered by Imam Nasir bin Murshid Al-Ya’rubi in the first half of the 17th century, or an earlier Portuguese fort watching the coast, the Wadi Al-Fulaij estuary and the inland road, captured by Omanis under Sultan bin Saif in 1648. It covers about 2,500 m², with walls about 55 m long and over 5 m high and four towers, three circular and one square, built to withstand cannon fire. Inside are a mosque with two mihrabs, a Qur’an classroom, a prison, a barzah hall, stores and a water reservoir; it was last restored in 1989.
sites.sig: The principal historic fort of Sur, a major Omani seafaring town.
sites.ex: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism (Experience Oman)
disc: Four towers: three round, one square

sites.s: 16th-century castle at Arabia’s easternmost point · teak ceilings from India
sites.dr: Construction began in the 16th century; restored 1989 and 2008
sites.el: Walls nearly 3 m thick; inner citadel over 13 m high
sites.te: The castle where the sun rises first
sites.se: At Ras Al Hadd, a stone castle guards the entrance of Khor Al-Hajar where the Sea of Oman meets the Arabian Sea
sites.sa: في رأس الحد يحرس حصن حجري مدخل خور الحجر حيث يلتقي بحر عُمان ببحر العرب
sites.desc: A castle in Ras Al Hadd, Wilayat of Sur, about 35 km from the town centre, on a plateau overlooking the entrance of Khor Al-Hajar at the meeting of the Sea of Oman and the Arabian Sea. Construction began in the 16th century with the participation of local tribes, and it served as a defensive centre and a place for tribal councils. Built of stone and gypsum, it has a main citadel and two towers linked by a wall nearly 3 m thick, a masabba for pouring hot liquids on attackers, cannons in the western tower and an inner citadel over 13 m high. Its ceilings use teak from India and timber from Mombasa and Zanzibar, and a passage of about 500 m is reported to lead to the Bir Marfas well; it was restored in 1989 and 2008.
sites.sig: A coastal stronghold whose timbers record Oman’s Indian Ocean trade links.

sites.na: كهف مقل في وادي بني خالد
sites.s: Karst cave with an underground river above the pools of Wadi Bani Khalid
sites.dr: Solution cave with ceiling boreholes attributed to hypogene speleogenesis; not dated
sites.el: Cave river flows even in dry periods
sites.se: Beyond the green pools of Wadi Bani Khalid, a low cave leads down to a river that never stops running
sites.sa: خلف برك وادي بني خالد الخضراء يقود كهف منخفض إلى نهر لا يتوقف عن الجريان
sites.desc: A karst cave in Wadi Bani Khalid, Ash Sharqiyah North, reached by a trail of about 500 m from a restaurant beside the wadi’s natural pools. Its passages are mostly wide and low, with one chamber high enough to stand in and a crawl descending at about 30° to a cave river that runs strongly even in dry periods. Almost circular vertical boreholes in the ceiling are attributed to hypogene speleogenesis, and the rear has wet sections with cave clay; a second, higher entrance is a vertical shaft. The cave likely floods during wadi floods.
sites.sig: Shows the groundwater system that feeds the perennial pools of Wadi Bani Khalid.
refs: Duckeck, J. Moqal Cave (مغارة مقل), Oman. Showcaves.com. https://showcaves.com/english/om/caves/Moqal.html
sites.conf: Coordinates from Showcaves.com; timeline is a broad Quaternary estimate because the cave is not dated; Showcaves gives the Arabic name as مغارة مقل

sites.s: Walled old quarter with fort, watchtowers and falaj in a ring of ophiolite hills · Al Qabil
sites.dr: Documented for the Ministry of Heritage and Culture in a 2014 heritage management plan
sites.el: Settlement core overlooked by Hisn al-Mudayrib
sites.se: Near Al Qabil, mud-and-stone houses, watchtowers and an old fort hide inside a ring of dark hills
sites.sa: قرب القابل تختبئ بيوت من الطين والحجر وأبراج مراقبة وحصن قديم داخل حلقة من التلال الداكنة
sites.desc: An old settlement in the Al Qabil area of Ash Sharqiyah North, set as a single core within a ring of low ophiolite hills and overlooked by Hisn al-Mudayrib, an enclosure-type fort. It was surveyed by ArCHIAM for the Ministry of Heritage and Culture, with a documentation and heritage management plan completed in 2014 that also covers its falaj channels and bathing structures. Watchtowers linked by walls crown the surrounding hills; villagers say they were built during the period of Portuguese incursions. Many houses belonged to sheikhs and have private wells, and the village is home to the Al Harthy tribe.
sites.sig: A well-documented example of a fortified Sharqiyah oasis quarter with its towers and falaj.
refs: ArCHIAM. Documentation and Heritage Management Plan: Harat al-Mudayrib, Al Qabil (2014). https://www.archiam.co.uk/documentation-and-heritage-management-plan-harat-al-mudayrib-al-qabil/
